transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-24 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE); Priya Anand (Redwood SE); Marcus Chen (Solutions); Elena Ruiz (Product); Lina Park (Head of ML, Atlas); Diego Morales (Platform Eng); Sasha Iqbal (CTO); Ravi Patel (SRE)

Auto-generated summary: Quick product walkthrough focused on long-context (12–16k), high TPS (target 5k), streaming backpressure and timeout behavior. Agreed to run a dedicated pilot with load tests and to share security docs.

Topics: long context handling; KV/prefix caching; batching strategies; streaming retries and backoff; dedicated vs hosted; VPC/KMS requirements; telemetry needed for SLOs.

[00:00] Jordan (AE): ok hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll keep this focused, this is titled concurrent long histories and stream throttling review, so we'll demo a few failure modes and then map them to configs you can flip in the console.

[00:28] Lina (Atlas): thanks Jordan, appreciate it. Quick context: Atlas runs a conversational assistant for retail support, avg session length is long — historically we push about 10–12k tokens per conversation and some enterprise customers are asking for 16k+ history. Peak TPS across all customers is about 4–5k, bursty with 30–40% at peak for checkout hours. Our SLO is p95 latency under 400ms for short responses, but for long-history we can accept higher — still want to avoid silent timeouts.

[01:05] Priya (SE): got it. we'll show three scenarios: 1) long prefix + KV cache hits, 2) concurrent high-TPS with streaming backpressure, 3) graceful degradation — model fallback and partial-history responses. We'll also pull up the console optimize suggestions.

[01:35] Diego (Atlas): one ask — we need to know what happens when the stream stalls for a minute, we had a previous incident where customers got an aborted response and the UI didn't recover.

[01:50] Marcus (Solutions): yeah, that's usually a case of queue saturation + chunking timeouts. Redwood's runtime does continuous batching and will snapshot KV caches, but if the per-gpu queue hits the hard limit, you'll see tail latencies and then streaming phases get dropped.

[02:20] Sasha (CTO): Do you have an offline mode or buffering to resume? We can't lose the whole response.

[02:32] Priya: we support streaming resume points via chunk ids in the protocol and prefix/KV cache rehydration, but the client needs to implement a reconnect-and-append flow. For many web SDKs we provide helpers. For immediate mitigation we often suggest: 1) enable prefix cache for stable parts of the history, 2) configure stream timeout longer than your UI's short poll, and 3) set a fallback policy to a smaller model variant so the response can be produced even under heavy load.

[03:10] Lina: smaller model variant — but will quality drop noticeably for our intent classification/slot-filling flows?

[03:22] Elena (Product): depends on the workload. For structured slot-filling we see limited degradation when moving from a 30B to a 7B quantized model if you keep the prompt engineering stable and use a reranker. For free-form generative content it's more visible. We can show a side-by-side.

[03:48] Jordan: I'm pulling up the console — this is the Optimize tab, it has suggested batching and quantization profiles based on your traffic. notice the recommendation for burst capacity and autoscale thresholds.

[04:20] [screen share noise — inaudible]

[04:35] Priya: demo time. scenario A: single conversation with 16k context where 80% is stable system messages and 20% is recent user turns. We'll show KV cache hits dramatically reducing token cost and latency.

[05:05] [06:00] Priya: starting request now — streaming enabled, chunk size 512 tokens. Expect first bytes in ~120ms if cache hits true.

[06:22] Lina: okay I see initial tokens arriving, nice. But what about memory blowup when many sessions keep KV in memory?

[06:36] Marcus: good question. we have configurable TTLs on per-session KV caches and a soft eviction policy — Optimize will recommend TTLs based on your session churn. For peak multi-tenant into dedicated pools we can pin sessions and evict cold sessions to S3-backed cold storage.

[07:05] Diego: are there controls to limit per-customer slot of KV memory? we don't want one big enterprise to starve others.

[07:15] Priya: yes, you can set per-tenant max-kv-entries and circuit limits in the routing policy. For dedicated that's especially easy — you get pools and can enforce tenant quotas.

[07:40] [08:00] Priya: moving to scenario B: high TPS synthetic replay. we'll push 5k sustained TPS with concurrent long contexts and measure queue depth, tail latencies and streaming drop rate.

[08:25] [08:50] Priya: test started — using the Atlas traffic pattern (Diego's CSV) with 30% long-history sessions, 70% short.

[09:10] Diego: logs are streaming in — I can see the first wave of 500 requests per second and then ramp.

[09:30] Priya: note the telemetry: per-route token breakdown, per-gpu queue depth. you'll see an inflection at 3.2k TPS where batching latency grows non-linearly.

[09:55] Sasha: why is batching latency growing — doesn't batching amortize cost?

[10:10] Marcus: it does, but continuous batching introduces a latency tradeoff: larger batch sizes increase throughput but also increase per-request wait time until the batch fills. With dynamic load spikes you get inconsistent batch fill times which increases tail latency.

[10:35] Priya: to counter this we demonstrated dynamic batch caps and per-route latency SLO knobs. the optimize engine suggests a per-route batch cap of 64 for your mix — that keeps p95 reasonable while sustaining higher throughput.

[11:05] [11:30] test results: at 5k TPS with default config we see p99 stream stalls at ~18 seconds and 3.6% of streams aborted by the client-side timeout. With tuned batch cap and prefix caching, p99 drops to ~4.2s and aborted streams to 0.6%.

[12:00] Lina: 18 seconds p99 is huge, that's our risk. What did you change exactly?

[12:15] Priya: batch cap from auto to 64, lower max-wait-ms to 60, enabled prefix caching for stable system prompts, and set a fallback policy to the 7B quantized tier when queue depth > 80%. Also increased streaming keepalive so clients don't time out prematurely.

[12:45] Diego: client timeouts were set to 10s on our end — we need to move to reconnect logic / longer streaming timeouts.

[13:00] Sasha: can Redwood do a graceful partial response — like deliver a condensed summary when full history would cause a timeout?

[13:12] Elena: yes, you can configure a progressive summary hook: if queue depth exceeds threshold the runtime will attempt to compress earlier turns into a short summary token block and continue. This reduces tokens and helps avoid whole-stream aborts. There are tradeoffs obviously.

[13:40] Lina: interesting. is that deterministic? we need to reproduce for audits.

[13:50] Priya: determinism depends on the summarizer model and seed. For compliance we recommend capturing the pre-summarized context in audit logs so you can replay. Redwood's console keeps the event trace with the summary hash.

[14:20] [15:00] Priya: moving to scenario C — simulated network flaps. we'll blackhole 1 out of 10 gpus for 30 seconds to see routing fallback.

[15:30] Marcus: you should see automatic reroute to compatible model variants and region fallback (if enabled). the system will prefer to maintain stream continuity by failing over to a capacity tier that meets latency SLOs, otherwise it will re-queue and apply backoff.

[16:05] [16:30] Diego: we're seeing reroutes but with small additional latency — that's acceptable if we don't drop connections. how about idempotency for retried streaming chunks?

[16:45] Priya: each chunk has a monotonic id and a last-applied token offset. clients can ack the last seen offset and the runtime will start sending from there. for exactly-once semantics you'll need your client ack/retry logic.

[17:10] Lina: security check — how does this interact with VPC/private? we can't have outbound keys leaving our net.

[17:22] Jordan: for Private deployments you can run the control plane inside your VPC and the inference plane on-prem, or we can do a VPC-peered hosted model. KMS integrations available; HSM on request. All traffic is TLS and you can enforce mutual TLS between your proxies and the runtime.

[17:50] Sasha: SOC 2 and ISO? audit logs?

[17:58] Elena: yes SOC 2 type II, ISO 27001, and audit-grade request/response logging with optional PII redaction hooks. we'll send the full security pack.

[18:20] [19:00] Priya: back to telemetry — the console shows token-level cost and per-route latency. for the 5k TPS test we keyed a dashboard that surfaced queue depth, model-switch events, and stream-abort counts. we can share the dashboard json.

[19:40] Diego: the dashboard looked useful. can we get alerts when stream-abort crosses 0.5%?

[19:50] Jordan: yes, alerting integrates with PagerDuty/Slack. you can set threshold-based alert rules on any metric.

[20:10] [21:00] Priya: demonstration of the client SDK reconnect snippet — shows re-open on transport error and resume from last chunk id. note: the snippet handles exponential backoff with jitter and an overall retry budget to avoid thundering herds.

[21:35] Lina: what about backpressure signalling from server to client? can you slow down the rate of tokens?

[21:45] Priya: we emit backpressure hints — a small header in the stream advising recommended client pacing, but the legal rate-limit is enforced by the server. The client can pause request generation until the hint clears.

[22:10] Sasha: are these hints compatible with our JS frontend?

[22:20] Marcus: yes, we've got a lightweight JS helper and a React hook. we can open-source a minimal wrapper.

[22:45] [23:15] Priya: now a quick failure-mode recap: 1) queue saturation — tune batch caps, autoscale, enable fallbacks; 2) KV memory pressure — TTLs, per-tenant quotas; 3) network flaps — chunk ids + reroute policies; 4) client timeouts — longer keepalive + reconnect; 5) heavy long-history — prefix caching + progressive summarization.

[24:10] Lina: nice summary. can you quantify cost delta when you enable prefix cache and batch tuning?

[24:30] Elena: roughly we saw token cost drop 18–32% depending on how much of the history is stable. In the benchmark we shared today cost per request dropped ~25% at 5k TPS after caching and quantization. We'll send the detailed sheet.

[25:00] Diego: is there an easy way to simulate our exact UX flows in your demo environment?

[25:10] Jordan: yes, we can import your CSV and run replay workloads into a staging pool. action: Diego will drop the CSV and we will run the 5k TPS pilot in a dedicated pool.

[25:40] [26:15] Diego: uploading CSV now... small pause... done.

[26:30] Priya: starting the replay with your profile. watch the routing page — you'll see per-tenant quotas and model switches.

[27:00] [27:45] test note: at 2.8k TPS we start to see queue depth accumulation — autoscale triggers and adds two workers; streaming latency improves. at 4.9k the autoscale is at cap, we hit fallback threshold and route some requests to quantized tier.

[28:20] Sasha: what's the cost implication of autoscale vs dedicated reservation?

[28:35] Elena: autoscale is pay-as-you-go so higher unit cost but elastic. reserved/dedicated gives lower unit cost and predictable throughput. often customers do a hybrid: reserved baseline and autoscale for bursts. We'll include a pricing sketch.

[29:00] [30:00] Priya: question from Ravi (SRE) about rehydration time: how long to restore a session KV after eviction?

[30:20] Marcus: depends on where it's stored; in-memory is instant, cold S3-backed rehydration can be a few hundred milliseconds to seconds depending on size; Optimize suggests partial rehydration of only active keys to reduce latency.

[31:00] Lina: curious about model warmup — when a new worker comes up, do you pre-warm the model? we've seen first-request cold start issues.

[31:15] Priya: yes, there's a configurable warmup. you can set a pool warmup policy to spool kernels and populate KV cache warm entries. For extremely tight SLOs we recommend keeping a small hot pool warm.

[31:50] [33:00] Priya: demo of console Rollouts — canary and A/B routing. showed a policy where 10% of requests go to the new quantized model for validation, and automatic rollback if quality regressions exceed threshold.

[33:35] Diego: we liked the regression guardrails — can they be connected to our evaluation set?

[33:45] Elena: yes, you can upload a golden prompt set and define quality thresholds. console will run lightweight evals on rollout and surface alerts.

[34:10] [35:00] Priya: quick note on logs: full request/response logging is available, with optional PII redaction and sampled payloads to meet retention needs. This ties into audit requirements.

[35:40] Lina: Good. Can we validate the PII redaction before pilot?

[35:50] Jordan: absolutely. we'll stand up a sandbox where you can test redaction rules.

[36:15] [37:00] Priya: I'm switching to a stress test where we gradually increase timeout aggressiveness to capture misbehaviors. At high load, clients that don't honor reconnects amplify backpressure. We recommend an overall retry budget plus randomized jitter.

[37:45] Lina: Are there recommended client SDK defaults for timeouts and retries?

[37:55] Marcus: yes — default retry budget 3 attempts, initial backoff 200ms with jitter, max per-request wall time 30s for streaming, and keepalive 60s. We'll provide the recommended snippet.

[38:30] [39:00] Priya: test end. summarizing today's key findings: with tuned batching, prefix caching and fallback enabled, Atlas should meet p95 latency objectives while staying within cost targets. There are two config changes on your side: increase client keepalive and implement reconnect/ack logic.

[39:40] Diego: we'll change the client timeouts. action: Diego to push that change to staging.

[40:00] Sasha: security follow up — when can we get the VPC peering checklist?

[40:08] Jordan: we'll email VPC checklist today and full security pack by EOD tomorrow.

[40:20] [41:00] Questions section:
Q: Will progressive summarization be auditable? A: yes, keep original context logs and summary hash.
Q: If a chunk is retried do tokens double-bill? A: billing deduplicates by chunk id for in-flight retries within retry budget.

[41:50] Lina: curious about long-term ops — do you provide runbooks?

[42:00] Elena: yes we'll provide an ops playbook with runbook actions, checklist items for scaling, and a dedicated contact for pilot.

[42:30] [43:00] Recap and explicit next steps:
- Redwood to run 5k TPS pilot on a dedicated pool using Atlas CSV (Priya & infra).
- Redwood to share pricing for dedicated + burst capacity (Jordan).
- Redwood to send security/VPC/KMS docs (Elena).
- Atlas to implement client reconnect & extend keepalive to 60s (Diego).
- Follow-up to review pilot results scheduled for 2027-09-07.

[45:10] Lina: sounds good. any blockers on our side? we'll need a signed MSA for dedicated at pilot start.

[45:30] Jordan: we can provide a pilot MSA template. Legal and procurement can fast-track a temporary addendum.

[46:00] [47:00] casual: uh thanks, appreciate the honest failure-mode demos.

[47:30] Marcus: one last tip — set conservative fallback thresholds early, you can loosen them later once telemetry looks stable.

[48:00] Diego: noted. we'll proceed.

[48:20] [49:00] Quick post-demo Q: does Red wood's runtime preserve original prompt tokens in the audit log or is it redacted by default?

[49:15] Elena: preserved by default but you can enable PII redaction. retention windows are configurable.

[49:45] Lina: perfect. thanks, team.

[50:00] [51:00] Jordan: OK we'll circle back. I'll send the pricing and runbook and Priya will run the bench. Thanks everyone, end of call.
